title: The Improbable Story of Martin Guerre
summary: Josh and Chuck retell the sixteenth-century French story of Martin Guerre: a Basque peasant from the Labourd region who abandoned his wife Bertrande de Rols and son, returned eight years later under the cover of Arnaud du Tilh, a Spanish impostor, and was accepted by his village and wife until his uncle Pierre accused him of fraud. The first trial in Rieux convicted the impostor, and the appellate Parliament of Toulouse case turned on Bertrande's testimony until the real Martin returned, the impostor was hanged and burned, and Bertrande was pardoned as having been duped. The hosts draw on Natalie Zemon Davis's book The Return of Martin Guerre and the 1982 film Le Retour de Martin Guerre (Summer's Be as the American remake). Also covers the Simpsons "Principal Skinner" reference and a closing request to rate and review the show.

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction
segments.summary: Hosts reminisce about college reading of Natalie Zemon Davis's book and introduce Martin Guerre; they discuss pronunciation and the Richard Gere confusion, the 1982 film Sommersby, and a Simpsons reference to a similar identity-swap story.

segments.title: Martin's origins and marriage
segments.summary: Martin Guerre is born to a Basque family that moves to France; the family rises into the merchant class and marries Martin at about thirteen or fourteen to Bertrande de Rols. The couple do not consummate the marriage for eight years, and remedies include masses and a cake. They then have a son.

segments.title: Martin leaves and goes to war
segments.summary: Martin is accused of stealing grain, does not defend himself, and abandons his wife and son. He goes to Spain, becomes a servant, joins the Spanish army, and loses a leg in battle.

segments.title: Bertrande's life in limbo and Natalie Zemon Davis's reinterpretation
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Bertrande's situation: she could not remarry without proof of death, her family cared for her, and Natalie Zemon Davis reframes her as a shrewd woman rather than a simple dupe.

segments.title: The impostor returns
segments.summary: Eight years later a man claiming to be Martin arrives at an inn, looking physically different but charming and knowing local stories. He stays at the inn claiming pox, retrieves white stockings from a chest to prove identity, and wins Bertrande and the town over.

segments.title: Pierre's opposition and the lawsuit
segments.summary: Uncle Pierre Guerre, who married Bertrande's mother, first accepts the man, then opposes him after a dispute over Martin's inheritance. Pierre's sons attempt to beat the man on the road and Bertrande shields him. The town splits, and Bertrande publicly backs him.

segments.title: Accusation of impostor and the first trial at Rieux
segments.summary: A Spanish soldier identifies the man as Arnaud du Tilh of Sahagún, a rough and bawdy man with a different foot size. At the trial at Rieux, the impostor cross-examines witnesses, including his sisters and Bertrande who testify for him, but the judge convicts him of fraud, adultery and theft and sentences him to death.

segments.title: Appeal to Parliament of Toulouse and the real Martin's return
segments.summary: On appeal, the judges favor the affirmative testimony that keeps the family intact, and the impostor forgives Bertrande on the stand. Just before the ruling, the real Martin Guerre appears with a wooden leg. His sisters and Bertrande recognize him, and Bertrande says she was duped. Martin says the wife ought to know her husband and blames only himself.

segments.title: Sentence, aftermath and legacy
segments.summary: Bertrande is not punished and her daughter's status is protected. Arnaud du Tilh is hanged and burned in front of Martin's house; he confesses and defends Bertrande. The hosts discuss the couple's later three sons and their uncertain relationship.

segments.title: Listener request to rate and review
segments.summary: Hosts ask listeners to tell friends about the show and to rate and review it on iTunes, Spotify, or wherever they listen.
